content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Technical Tutorial: Black Box Testing Techniques - Equivalence Partitioning & Boundary Value Analysis"},{"order":2,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Introduction to Black Box Testing"},{"order":3,"type":"paragraph","text":"Black box testing is a software testing method where the internal system design, code structure, and implementation details are hidden from the tester. Testing is performed entirely based on requirements and functional specifications. Two of the most powerful and systematic black box test design techniques are Equivalence Partitioning (EP) and Boundary Value Analysis (BVA)."},{"order":4,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Equivalence Partitioning (EP)"},{"order":5,"type":"paragraph","text":"Equivalence Partitioning is a specification-based technique where input data to a software component is divided into distinct partitions or classes of data from which test cases can be derived. The core principle behind EP is that test cases designed to test a representative value of each class are expected to exhibit the same behavior as all other values within that same class."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Valid Equivalence Partitions: Represent the correct, accepted inputs that the system is designed to process successfully."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Invalid Equivalence Partitions: Represent incorrect, erroneous, or unexpected inputs that should trigger error handling mechanisms."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Practical Example of Equivalence Partitioning"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Consider an input field for an Age validator that accepts values from 18 to 60 inclusive. We can divide this into three partitions:"},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Invalid Partition 1 (Too Young): Age < 18 (e.g., 15)"},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Valid Partition (Allowed): 18 <= Age <= 60 (e.g., 30)"},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Invalid Partition 2 (Too Old): Age > 60 (e.g., 65)"},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Boundary Value Analysis (BVA)"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"Boundary Value Analysis builds upon Equivalence Partitioning. Experience shows that a greater proportion of software defects occur at the boundaries or edges of equivalence partitions rather than within the center. BVA focuses on testing the boundary values of these partitions, including minimum, maximum, just below, and just above the thresholds."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"For a range [Min, Max], the standard BVA test cases for a single variable are: Min, Min-plus-1, Just below Min (if invalid), Max, Max-minus-1, and Just above Max (if invalid)."},{"order":16,"type":"subheading","text":"Practical Example of Boundary Value Analysis"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"Using the same Age validator range [18, 60], the BVA test values include:"},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"17 (Boundary value just below the lower limit - Invalid)"},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"18 (Lower boundary value - Valid)"},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"19 (Value just above the lower boundary - Valid)"},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"59 (Value just below the upper boundary - Valid)"},{"order":22,"type":"bullet_point","text":"60 (Upper boundary value - Valid)"},{"order":23,"type":"bullet_point","text":"61 (Boundary value just above the upper limit - Invalid)"},{"order":24,"type":"subheading","text":"4. Summary and Best Practices for Manual Testers"},{"order":25,"type":"paragraph","text":"Combining Equivalence Partitioning and Boundary Value Analysis provides a rigorous approach to black box testing. EP minimizes the total number of test cases by eliminating redundancy, while BVA targets the most error-prone areas of software logic. Always document your partitions explicitly in your test strategy before executing test cases."}]
